g.title: N2 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) exemplifies this approach by sampling multiple chain-of-thought reasoning paths (Wei et al., 2022) and aggregating answers via majority vote, achieving substantial accuracy gains over single-sample inference.

g.title: N3 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, this effectiveness comes at significant computational cost: generating multiple complete reasoning chains requires proportionally more tokens, making self-consistency expensive for deployment at scale.

g.title: N5 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Confidence-guided early stopping (Aghazadeh et al., 2025) terminates sampling once the posterior probability of the majority answer exceeds a threshold.

g.title: N6 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Slim-SC (Hong et al., 2025) prunes redundant reasoning chains online using thought embedding similarity.

g.title: N7 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) ESC (Li et al., 2024) applies early stopping based on window vote entropy.

g.text: While effective, these approaches fundamentally discard partial

g.title: N8 [Limitation] (cites=0) While effective, these approaches fundamentally discard partial reasoning—they stop sampling entirely rather than leveraging the information contained in incomplete chains.

g.text: This raises a natural question: can we identify promising reasoning paths
early and focus continuation budget on them?
g.title: N9 [Limitation] (cites=0) This raises a natural question: can we identify promising reasoning paths early and focus continuation budget on them?

g.text: We investigate this question through Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency
(DCS), a two-stage approach that attempts to improve token efficiency by
allocating continuation budget to promising branches identified through
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) We investigate this question through Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency (DCS), a two-stage approach that attempts to improve token efficiency by allocating continuation budget to promising branches identified through early voting signals.

g.text: In Stage 1, DCS samples B = 7 draft solutions with a token limit Tdraft =
1024, extracts interim answers, and computes a vote histogram.
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) In Stage 1, DCS samples B = 7 draft solutions with a token limit Tdraft = 1024, extracts interim answers, and computes a vote histogram.

g.text: In Stage 2, it selects k = 3 branches from high-vote answers and continues
them for an additional Tcont = 1024 tokens, using a hedge allocation
strategy that reserves one slot for the second-place answer to guard against
g.title: N12 [Method] (cites=0) In Stage 2, it selects k = 3 branches from high-vote answers and continues them for an additional Tcont = 1024 tokens, using a hedge allocation strategy that reserves one slot for the second-place answer to guard against early consensus errors.

than standard self-consistency and 109% more than CGES-LNS, which
g.title: N13 [Result] (cites=0) Our experiments on MATH-500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct reveal a negative result: DCS matches baseline accuracy (76.8%) but uses 19.6% more tokens than standard self-consistency and 109% more than CGES-LNS, which Pareto-dominates DCS on the accuracy-efficiency frontier.

g.title: N14 [Result] (cites=0) Analysis reveals that approximately 96% of drafts complete naturally within the token limit, causing the continuation mechanism to rarely activate meaningfully.

g.text: two-stage approach that attempts to improve efficiency by

g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We introduce Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency (DCS), a two-stage approach that attempts to improve efficiency by continuing promising branches rather than stopping early.

g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We conduct rigorous experiments on MATH-500 comparing DCS against greedy decoding, uniform self-consistency, and confidence-guided early stopping.

g.text: We report a negative result with detailed analysis: DCS fails to
improve efficiency because high draft completion rates (∼96%)

g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We report a negative result with detailed analysis: DCS fails to improve efficiency because high draft completion rates (∼96%) undermine the continuation mechanism, demonstrating that simpler early-stopping methods dominate two-stage approaches when draft budgets are sufficient.
